title: Urbanismo y Construcción (3a ed.)
author: Juan Eduardo Figueroa Valdés
english_translation: Urban Planning and Construction (3rd ed.)
annotation: It covers the ground where public law meets land use and the physical growth of cities. That is where I can connect legal rules to the way urban form and transportation actually develop.

title: Diego Portales y la tradición política portaliana
author: Gonzalo Arenas Hoder
english_translation: Diego Portales and the Portalian Political Tradition
annotation: I don't share Portales's worldview, but his ideas about order, authority and the elite project of 'civilizing' the poor left a lasting mark on Chilean political culture. Knowing where they came from makes it easier to spot the assumptions about hierarchy and state authority that still turn up in Chilean public life.

title: Roman Law and the Legal World of the Romans
author: Andrew M. Riggsby
annotation: Riggsby puts Roman law back inside the society and institutions that produced it, so legal development reads as part of a working political and social order.

title: Historia Social, Política y Jurídica de Roma
author: Carlos Felipe Amunátegui Perelló
english_translation: Social, Political, and Legal History of Rome
annotation: I like how Amunátegui ties Roman law to political and social change, so that legal authority and its institutions grow up alongside the Roman state.

title: Vicios del acto administrativo
author: Fabián Huepe Artigas; Baltazar Morales Espinoza; Francisco Santibañez Yáñez
english_translation: Flaws in Administrative Acts
annotation: Chile is where I learned to work with legal logic in practice. Defective administrative acts raise the questions that shaped that experience: who was competent to act, whether the act was legal, whether procedure was followed and where public authority stops.

title: Introducción a la historia del derecho chileno: Constitución, legalidad y cultura jurídica, siglos XVI a XX
author: Fernando Muñoz León
english_translation: Introduction to the History of Chilean Law: Constitution, Legality, and Legal Culture, 16th to 20th Centuries
annotation: Knowing the history of Chilean law helps me make sense of the legal and political assumptions I ran into while working there. Living in Chile has also left me feeling responsible for understanding its institutions as the product of a long legal and political history.

title: La motivación: Principio general del derecho público
author: Alejandro Gómez Sotomayor
english_translation: Reasoning: A General Principle of Public Law
annotation: Reason-giving is where administrative legality, accountability and judicial review meet. The book also explains a good part of the civil-law approach to public law, which became far more familiar to me working in Chile than it ever was growing up in the United States.

title: El impulso sistemático del derecho administrativo chileno (1861-1890)
author: Gabriel Bocksang Hola
english_translation: The Systematic Impetus of Chilean Administrative Law (1861–1890)
annotation: Bocksang shows how Chilean administrative law was organized into a coherent system of concepts between 1861 and 1890. That history explains a lot about the legal mindset I absorbed working on regulation and public administration in Chile.

title: Historia del Derecho: Evolución de las fuentes del derecho privado occidental en sus textos y contextos, de la romanización a la codificación
author: Italo Merello Arecco
english_translation: History of Law: The Evolution of the Sources of Western Private Law in Their Texts and Contexts, from Romanization to Codification
annotation: Merello covers the whole stretch from Romanization to codification, which is long enough to show how the civil-law tradition became systematic and attentive to its sources. The common-law environment I grew up around in the United States works differently on both counts.

title: El Estado sobre ruedas: Transporte público, política y ciudad. La ETCE 1945-1981
author: Simón Castillo; Marcelo Mardones; Waldo Vila
english_translation: The State on Wheels: Public Transport, Politics, and the City, ETCE 1945–1981
annotation: My interest in transit goes beyond work. It is how I think about governance, urban development and the relationship between land use and transportation, and this book puts all of those questions into one Chilean historical case.

title: The Great Society Subway: A History of the Washington Metro
author: Zachary M. Schrag
annotation: I read it as a history of transit as governance. Schrag shows institutions, regional politics, planning decisions, financing and land-use ambitions coming together in one of the most important postwar public transport projects in the United States.

title: Megaprojects and Risk: An Anatomy of Ambition
author: Bent Flyvbjerg; Nils Bruzelius; Werner Rothengatter
annotation: Big infrastructure projects show how governments and institutions decide things under uncertainty. The book's account of optimism bias, strategic misrepresentation and project risk is directly relevant to how I think about transport and public investment.

title: As I Lay Dying
author: William Faulkner
annotation: Faulkner tells the story in many voices, each with a partial view. Family, place, memory and social surroundings all come through that way, and no single account gets to be the authoritative one.

title: La Regenta
author: Leopoldo Alas (Clarín)
english_translation: The Regent's Wife
annotation: It is a major work of realism and also a close study of a provincial society: its hierarchy, religion, reputation and institutional pressure. Clarín shows in unusual detail how a social order keeps reproducing itself.

title: A History of Babylon, 2200 BC–AD 75
author: Paul-Alain Beaulieu
annotation: Babylon fascinates me because it is so old and lasted so long. Beaulieu makes people and institutions from that far back feel understandable, and shows political authority surviving and changing over more than two thousand years.

title: A History of the Ancient Near East, ca. 3000-323 BC (2nd ed.)
author: Marc Van De Mieroop
annotation: This is my chronological frame for the ancient Near East. When I read about a particular ruler, state, administrative system or cultural shift, this is where I go to place it in a regional history that runs across thousands of years.

title: Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia, Volume I: Historical Records of Assyria from the Earliest Times to Sargon
author: Daniel David Luckenbill
annotation: Primary records close some of the distance between us and these very old states. Reading how Assyrian rulers described their own power, administration, wars and legitimacy makes me think about what has changed in political life since then, and what hasn't.

title: Assyria: The Rise and Fall of the World's First Empire
author: Eckart Frahm
annotation: Assyria interests me as an early imperial state, and as a society whose rulers could be conquerors, administrators, builders on a huge scale and curious intellectuals all at once. Figures like Ashurbanipal are a good reminder that the pursuit of knowledge is not a modern habit.

title: Entrepreneurs and Enterprise in Early Mesopotamia: A Study of Three Archives from the Third Dynasty of Ur (2112–2004 BCE)
author: Steven J. Garfinkle
annotation: Administrative and economic archives make the ancient world concrete in a way I didn't expect. These three archives from Ur III are full of enterprise, contracts, accounts and people taking initiative, all of it recognizable, inside a state more than four thousand years old.

title: Gudea and His Dynasty
author: Dietz Otto Edzard
annotation: I genuinely admire Gudea. His idea of kingship centers on building, piety, stewardship and orderly government, and those aims still feel recognizable after more than four thousand years.

title: Hammurabi of Babylon
author: Dominique Charpin
annotation: Hammurabi is famous as a lawgiver. Charpin also treats him as a ruler, which lets me follow how state authority, administration and justice developed, and how law related to political power.

title: Hezekiah in History and Tradition
author: Robb Andrew Young
annotation: Young keeps two Hezekiahs in view: the king historians can reconstruct and the one later tradition remembered. Texts, archaeology and political tradition each preserve a somewhat different version of the same past.

title: History Begins at Sumer: 27 Firsts in Recorded History
author: Samuel Noah Kramer
annotation: Kramer makes it vivid how old organized human life is. Newer scholarship complicates some of his 'firsts', but the main point holds: institutions, literature, schooling, conflict and humor were already there in Sumer.

title: Israel's Past Seen from the Present: Studies on History and Religion in Ancient Israel and Judah
author: Bob Becking
annotation: Becking keeps historical memory in view the whole time: how later communities rebuilt their own past, and how our assumptions today shape what we think ancient history means.

title: King Hammurabi of Babylon: A Biography
author: Marc Van De Mieroop
annotation: I read this alongside the legal histories. Van De Mieroop brings back Hammurabi the politician and administrator, and his laws become one piece of a larger project that also involved state-building, diplomacy, war and governance.

title: Leadership in the Ancient World: Concepts, Models, Theories
author: Melina Tamiolaki (editor)
annotation: Part of what draws me to ancient history is finding familiar ambitions, virtues, weaknesses and political problems in societies that lived an enormously long time ago. Comparing leaders across the ancient world is a direct way to look for them.

title: Networks of Authority and Power in Ur III Times
author: Piotr Michalowski
annotation: I'm interested in Ur III mostly for its early state administration. Michalowski rebuilds authority from the networks, officials, institutions and documents, which is more useful to me than treating the state as an abstract, centralized machine.

title: Sennacherib, King of Assyria
author: Josette Elayi
annotation: A biography of a single Assyrian king makes imperial administration and strategy concrete. With Sennacherib you can watch military power, state organization, building projects and royal self-presentation working together.

title: Sennacherib at the Gates of Jerusalem: Story, History and Historiography
author: Isaac Kalimi; Seth Richardson (editors)
annotation: Sennacherib's campaign against Jerusalem can be seen through Assyrian sources, biblical memory, archaeology and later historians. That makes it a good case for studying how historical memory gets made and argued over.

title: The Age of Agade: Inventing Empire in Ancient Mesopotamia
author: Benjamin R. Foster
annotation: Agade was an early experiment in imperial power. The subtitle's phrase, 'inventing empire', gets at what I want to know: how people first built the administrative and ideological tools to govern something larger than a city-state.

title: The Oxford History of the Ancient Near East, Volume III: From the Hyksos to the Late Second Millennium BC
author: Karen Radner; Nadine Moeller; D. T. Potts (editors)
annotation: This is my reference for the period when the ancient Near East became closely interconnected. States in this volume are understood through their dealings with one another: diplomacy, migration, trade, war and rival systems of authority.

title: The Passionate Bureaucrat: Lessons for the 21st Century from 4,500 Years of Public Service Reform
author: Max Everest-Phillips
annotation: I think of administration as a problem people keep running into. I like seeing questions of bureaucracy, implementation, reform and public service traced back 4,500 years instead of treated as modern problems.

title: The Sumerians: Their History, Culture and Character
author: Samuel Noah Kramer
annotation: Kramer's classic synthesis covers what fascinates me most about the ancient Near East. Sumer's cities and states are about as early as it gets, and they are full of institutions, ambitions and anxieties that are still surprisingly easy to recognize.

title: Clement of Alexandria: The Exhortation to the Greeks; The Rich Man's Salvation; To the Newly Baptized
author: Clement of Alexandria
annotation: Reading Clement himself shows me how an early Christian explained his beliefs, his ethics and his place in the Greco-Roman world, without going through later summaries.

title: Justin Martyr: His Life and Thought
author: L. W. Barnard
annotation: Justin interests me because he stood between Christianity and classical philosophy and tried to work out the terms between them. Barnard shows early Christianity as an intellectual movement that grew up inside the Greco-Roman world.

title: The Apostolic Fathers: Greek Texts and English Translations
author: Michael W. Holmes (editor and translator)
annotation: These are the primary sources I start from for Christianity right after the New Testament period, when it was still diverse and its institutions were taking shape.

title: The Jesus Movement: A Social History of Its First Century
author: Ekkehard W. Stegemann; Wolfgang Stegemann
annotation: The Stegemanns write social history, so early Christianity appears among real communities, institutions, class structures and political conditions. Doctrine is only part of the story.

title: The Jesus Movement and the World of the Early Church
author: Sheila E. McGinn
annotation: McGinn describes the social and historical setting in which the Jesus movement turned into communities and institutions that lasted.

title: The Moral Psychology of Clement of Alexandria: Mosaic Philosophy
author: Kathleen Gibbons
annotation: Gibbons works at the level of moral psychology and philosophy, showing how Clement and other Christian thinkers took in the intellectual traditions around them, adapted them and pushed back against them.

title: La esquina es mi corazón
author: Pedro Lemebel
english_translation: The Corner Is My Heart
annotation: Lemebel's Chile is intimate, urban and marginal, and it is deliberately nothing like the official political or institutional history. He makes me look at the lives and places that more conventional histories leave at the edges.

title: Balmaceda: Su Gobierno y la Revolución de 1891
author: Julio Bañados Espinosa
english_translation: Balmaceda: His Government and the Revolution of 1891
annotation: Chile's civil war of 1891 holds a very different place in national memory than the American Civil War does in the United States. Getting Balmaceda's real role straight shows me how an event with large consequences can fade almost out of popular memory.

title: Historia del Derecho
author: Jaime Eyzaguirre
english_translation: History of Law
annotation: Eyzaguirre is part of how I've been learning the history behind the legal tradition I met professionally in Chile, especially its assumptions about sources, institutions and legal order, which don't always match an American common-law background.

title: La guerra civil de 1891, Tomo 1: La irrupción política de los militares en Chile
author: Alejandro San Francisco
english_translation: The Civil War of 1891, Volume 1: The Political Intervention of the Military in Chile
annotation: Part of the fascination is the gap between how much the 1891 war mattered and how little most people remember it. Studying it closely explains the political order that came after, and how Chile remembers its internal conflicts, or doesn't.

title: La guerra del Pacífico (1879–1883)
author: Carmen McEvoy; Gabriel Cid
english_translation: The War of the Pacific (1879–1883)
annotation: You can't understand Chilean national identity, territorial memory or Chile's relations with its neighbors without the War of the Pacific. What the war became in public culture afterward matters almost as much as the war itself.

title: Labradores, peones y proletarios: Formación y crisis de la sociedad popular chilena del siglo XIX
author: Gabriel Salazar Vergara
english_translation: Farmers, Peons, and Proletarians: Formation and Crisis of Chilean Popular Society in the 19th Century
annotation: Salazar looks past the elites and institutions to how Chile's popular classes formed, and I don't think the country's history makes sense without that. He also gives social context for the nineteenth-century political language of order, civilization and hierarchy.

title: Anarchy, State, and Utopia
author: Robert Nozick
annotation: Nozick makes a rigorous argument about the moral limits of state power. I don't accept all of his conclusions, but he makes me test what I assume about coercion, redistribution, rights and how far government should reach.

title: And the Band Played On: Politics, People, and the AIDS Epidemic
author: Randy Shilts
annotation: What I study in the AIDS crisis is political and institutional failure. Shilts shows delay, fragmented authority, incentives, bureaucracy, stigma and individual decisions adding up to a public policy catastrophe.

title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
author: Hannah Arendt
annotation: Arendt raises hard questions about responsibility, obedience and judgment, and about how ordinary bureaucratic behavior can have extraordinary moral consequences.

title: How to Survive a Plague: The Inside Story of How Citizens and Science Tamed AIDS
author: David France
annotation: I read it next to the histories of institutional failure. France shows organized citizens, activists and scientists forcing change when existing systems were failing, with public institutions eventually coming along.

title: Last Days of the SFRY
author: Borisav Jovic
annotation: This is an insider's account of a state coming apart. From inside the government you see politicians interpreting events, misreading each other and helping to unravel structures they had assumed would last.

title: Patient Zero and the Making of the AIDS Epidemic
author: Richard A. McKay
annotation: McKay traces how one powerful, misleading story shaped what the public understood about an epidemic. It adds the history of the narrative to my interest in institutional failure, since institutions and the media also build stories about who is to blame.

title: Public Transit Planning and Operation: Theory, Modeling and Practice
author: Avishai (Avi) Ceder
annotation: I use it for work and for my own interest. Ceder covers the technical side of transit planning and operations, which complements my broader interest in how governance, urban form and land use shape a transit system.

title: Transporte Público: Planeación, diseño, operación y administración
author: Ángel R. Molinero Molinero; Ignacio Sánchez Arellano
english_translation: Public Transport: Planning, Design, Operation, and Administration
annotation: This is my Spanish-language technical reference. It connects planning, design, operation and administration, the practical parts of public transport that sit underneath the governance and land-use questions I'm interested in.

title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor E. Frankl
annotation: Frankl writes about meaning, dignity and agency in extreme conditions. It's a book I end up reflecting on personally, more than one I simply agree or disagree with.

title: The Practicing Stoic: A Philosophical User's Manual
author: Ward Farnsworth
annotation: My interest in Stoicism is separate from my interest in early Christianity. Farnsworth organizes Stoic thought around practical problems of judgment, emotion, desire, adversity and conduct, so it reads as something to use and not only as an ancient philosophical system.

title: Enchiridion
author: Epictetus
annotation: Epictetus draws the line between what is and isn't in our control very directly. The book is short enough that Stoicism feels like a discipline of judgment and conduct, something you practice.

title: Marcus Agrippa: A Biography
author: Meyer Reinhold
annotation: Agrippa complicates the usual story of the Augustan age, which centers on the ruler. His career shows administration, military skill, engineering, loyalty and personal relationships mattering as much as formal sovereignty.

title: Marcus Agrippa: Right-hand Man of Caesar Augustus
author: Lindsay Powell
annotation: Agrippa is a case of real power exercised from beside the top instead of from it. He was good at war, administration and infrastructure, and that combination is exactly what interests me.

title: Marcus Aurelius: A Life
author: Frank McLynn
annotation: McLynn puts the philosopher-emperor back into his working life of governing, war, family and imperial administration. The Meditations read differently once you know the life they came out of.

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
annotation: My interest here is Stoic, not Christian. I like that the text is private and repetitive. It shows Marcus using philosophy day after day to correct himself, judge carefully and hold back.

title: The Cambridge History of Greek and Roman Political Thought
author: Christopher Rowe; Malcolm Schofield (editors)
annotation: I go to this for how the Greeks and Romans thought about authority, citizenship, law, constitutions, virtue and political order. Those ideas kept shaping Western legal and political traditions long afterward.

title: Southern Honor: Ethics and Behavior in the Old South
author: Bertram Wyatt-Brown
annotation: Wyatt-Brown treats the antebellum South as a social and moral system with its own codes of status, reputation, violence and hierarchy. A lot of behavior that makes no sense through formal politics alone makes sense through those codes.

title: The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order
author: Samuel P. Huntington
annotation: I don't read this as a framework to adopt. It's an influential argument, and I want to understand it on its own terms. It's also a good test case for big claims about culture, identity and geopolitical conflict, and for the risks of treating civilizations as coherent political actors.

title: Región y nación: la construcción provincial de Chile, siglo XIX
author: Armando Cartes Montory
english_translation: Region and nation: the provincial construction of Chile in the 19th century
annotation: Cartes shows Chile's state and national identity being built through its regions, which is a useful corrective to seeing everything from Santiago outward. It gives today's tensions between the capital and the regions a history.

title: Santiago de Chile (1541-1991): Historia de una sociedad urbana
author: Armando de Ramón
english_translation: Santiago, Chile (1541-1991): a history of an urban society
annotation: Santiago makes more sense once you see its present shape as the result of 450 years of social, political, economic and spatial change. It also connects to my interest in land use, transportation and governance.

title: Historia de Chile: Desde la invasión incaica hasta nuestros días (1500-2000)
author: Armando de Ramón
english_translation: History of Chile: from the Incan invasion until the present (1500-2000)
annotation: As an immigrant, I think knowing Chilean history well is a civic responsibility. The news makes far more sense against the long development of the country's institutions, political identities, regional differences and recurring ideas about authority and order.

title: Tocqueville's Nightmare: The Administrative State Emerges in America, 1900–1940
author: Daniel R. Ernst
annotation: I grew up in the United States with common-law assumptions in the background, and I learned to think seriously about regulation inside Chile's more continental legal culture. Ernst shows how the American administrative state worked out its own answer to that tension.

title: Controlling Administrative Power: An Historical Comparison
author: Peter Cane
annotation: Cane compares legal traditions at exactly the point I care about most: how each one thinks about administrative power, limits it and justifies courts reviewing it. Reading him, I can sort out which of my legal instincts came from working in Chile and which came from growing up in the U.S.

title: La teoría general del Derecho administrativo como sistema
author: Eberhard Schmidt-Assmann
english_translation: General Theory of Administrative Law as a System
annotation: Schmidt-Assmann spells out the systematic, conceptual style of administrative-law reasoning that became second nature to me in Chile. Read comparatively, it also shows why that way of thinking can sound so European to an American lawyer.

title: The Roman Law Tradition
author: A. D. E. Lewis; D. J. Ibbetson (editors)
annotation: The way Roman law was received and reinterpreted over the centuries is how the continental tradition got its concepts, categories and habits of thought, and those eventually reached systems like Chile's.

title: Comparative Law
author: Uwe Kischel
annotation: Kischel gave me words for something I had lived before I had a framework for it. Growing up around American common-law assumptions and then learning legal logic through real work in Chile meant living with two different ways of organizing and reasoning about law.

title: A Natural History of the Common Law
author: S. F. C. Milsom
annotation: Milsom lets me look at the common law from the inside, as a tradition with a history, where I used to take it as the American default I grew up with. His focus on law developing through adjudication means more to me after working in a more systematized civil-law setting.

title: An Historical Introduction to Private Law
author: R. C. van Caenegem
annotation: This is a bridge between the two legal worlds I know. Van Caenegem explains historically why English common law and continental private law went different ways, and he doesn't settle for the usual shorthand of precedent versus codes.

title: Historical Foundations of the Common Law
author: S. F. C. Milsom
annotation: The common law was culturally familiar to me in the United States, but I never had to analyze it as consciously as the Chilean system I later worked in. Milsom gives me its history in depth.

title: Historia del Derecho privado de la Edad Moderna
author: Franz Wieacker
english_translation: History of Private Law in the Modern Era
annotation: Wieacker traces where modern civil law came from intellectually: the reception of Roman law, legal science, natural law, codification and system-building. That lineage explains the style of legal thinking I worked with in Chile.

title: European Legal History: A Cultural and Political Perspective
author: Randall Lesaffer
annotation: Lesaffer writes legal history as part of political and cultural history. That gives me the background for why the European traditions Latin America inherited turned out the way they did.

title: El orden jurídico medieval
author: Paolo Grossi
english_translation: The Medieval Legal Order
annotation: It's easy to assume law has always been codified and centered on the state. Grossi's medieval Europe had a plural legal order, and once you've seen it, modern civil-law systems look like something people built at a particular time.

title: Mitología jurídica de la modernidad
author: Paolo Grossi
english_translation: Legal Mythology of Modernity
annotation: Grossi takes ideas that seem obvious, like state sovereignty over law, codification and the completeness of the legal order, and shows that they are historically contingent. I lean on that when comparing the civil-law mindset I learned in Chile with the common-law world I grew up in.
